title: Social Sciences · Seq 6 Inequality in health access

questions.stem: Health inequity, as opposed to health inequality, refers to differences that are:
options: Due only to natural variation such as age
Avoidable
Unjust
Unfair
questions.explanation: Differences due to natural variation (older vs younger adults) are inequalities, not necessarily injustices.

questions.stem: Older adults generally have different health needs than younger adults. According to the course, this is:
options: An inequality, but not necessarily an injustice
A structural barrier
An example of the Inverse Care Law
A health inequity
questions.explanation: The course's example of a health inequality that is not an inequity.

questions.stem: Dimensions of access to healthcare listed in the course:
options: Genetic access — inherited ability to recover
Cultural access — linguistically and culturally appropriate services
Financial access — ability to afford care, medicines and transport
Geographic access — physical distance to facilities
questions.explanation: The five dimensions: geographic, financial, cultural, timely, quality.

questions.stem: The Inverse Care Law:
options: States that the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need for it
States that the poorest receive the most care
Operates more completely where medical care is most exposed to market forces
Was first described by Julian Tudor Hart in 1971
questions.explanation: Those who need healthcare most are the least likely to receive it.

questions.stem: People in the countries with the lowest life expectancy live, compared with those in the highest:
options: 33 years less
5 years less
41 years less
17 years less
questions.explanation: A 33-year gap, reflecting inequalities in healthcare, water, nutrition and social conditions.

questions.stem: In Canada (Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging), greater difficulty accessing specialist care was associated with:
options: Lacking a family physician
Household income below $50,000
Living in a rural area
Having universal health coverage
questions.explanation: Even with universal healthcare, disparities persist by income, race, immigrant status and Indigeneity.

questions.stem: Key facts about low- and middle-income countries given in the course:
options: Low-income countries spend about $17 per capita per year on health
Stockouts of essential NCD medicines affect up to 41% of low-income countries vs 4% of high-income ones
Asia and Africa show the most significant intraregional inequalities in maternal and child health
Government health spending is projected to rise in all low-income countries by 2030
questions.explanation: Over 80% of low-income countries are projected to spend less on health in 2030 than in 2024.

questions.stem: By the end of 2021, the share of people with at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose was:
options: 5.4% in low-income countries
64.1% in low-income countries
5.4% in high-income countries
64.1% in high-income countries
questions.explanation: "Vaccine nationalism" reflected policy choices favouring profit and national interest.

questions.stem: Match the financial cost to its type:
options: Hidden costs — healthy food and lifestyle expenses
Indirect costs — transportation and lost wages
Hidden costs — hospital fees
Direct costs — consultations, medicines, hospital fees
questions.explanation: Hospital fees are direct costs.

questions.stem: Social and cultural barriers to health access include:
options: Stigma associated with illnesses such as HIV and mental disorders
Immigration-related difficulties
Poor roads and inadequate infrastructure
Language difficulties
questions.explanation: Poor roads are a geographic barrier.

questions.stem: Systemic and structural barriers include:
options: Weak governance and lack of accountability
Shortage of healthcare professionals
Hidden lifestyle costs
Poor coordination between healthcare services
questions.explanation: Also inadequate health information systems. Hidden costs are financial barriers.

questions.stem: The "poverty trap" described among the consequences of unequal access means:
options: Rich countries lose productivity
Childhood illness has no later effects
Illness increases poverty, while poverty limits healthcare access
Poor people use emergency services less
questions.explanation: One of the economic and social consequences, with lost productivity and intergenerational effects.

questions.stem: Limited access to preventive care puts pressure on healthcare systems through:
options: Greater use of emergency services
Fewer patients reaching hospitals
Less investment in prevention and early diagnosis
Higher treatment costs
questions.explanation: Section 4.3.

questions.stem: In the Pakistan vs Canada case study:
options: Canada faces gaps in achieving equal access for everyone
Pakistan struggles mainly with basic healthcare infrastructure
Indigenous children in Canada face greater health risks
Canada has no universal healthcare
questions.explanation: Canada's universal healthcare reduces financial barriers, but inequalities remain.

questions.stem: Among older homeless adults in Chicago:
options: Only 66% of those needing medical assistance obtained it
Most received dental care easily
Arthritis, diabetes, hypertension and vision problems were frequent
Only 18% of those needing dental assistance received it
questions.explanation: Age, homelessness and poverty combine to increase inequalities.

questions.stem: In the study of women living with chronic STDs, the most frequent type of healthcare interaction was:
options: Moral surveillance (42%)
Moral surveillance (27%)
The patient-centred approach (31%)
The biomedical approach (42%)
questions.explanation: Biomedical 42% (disease rather than the person), patient-centred 31%, moral surveillance 27%.

questions.stem: Health equity is based on four principles:
options: Justice — fair distribution of resources
Solidarity — shared responsibility
Profitability — care driven by market forces
Accountability and participation
questions.explanation: Accountability = monitoring healthcare systems; participation = involving communities in decisions.

questions.stem: About the Algerian healthcare system:
options: It is a dual system with a public and a growing private sector
Health spending is about 5.2% of GDP
Life expectancy reached 76 years in 2024
Maternal mortality rose between 1999 and 2019
questions.explanation: Maternal mortality fell from 117.4 to 48.5 per 100,000 births (1999–2019).

questions.stem: The Boussemghoun study (2025) of 400 adults found that:
options: Access to dental and mental health services was high
36.5% travelled to other regions for healthcare
52.3% did not visit a general practitioner during the previous year
39.7% had at least one chronic disease
questions.explanation: Access to mental health, dental and preventive services was particularly low.

questions.stem: About the El-Chifa card:
options: It provides health insurance coverage in Algeria
It removes all indirect costs such as transport
Insurance alone does not guarantee access when local services are inadequate
It includes full coverage for certain chronic-disease prescriptions
questions.explanation: Even with free public care, transport, lost wages and accommodation remain indirect barriers.

questions.stem: Recent Algerian policy responses cited by the course:
options: Creation of a Ministry of Pharmaceutical Industry
Second National Cancer Plan (2025–2030)
Increased healthcare budget in the 2025 Finance Law
Privatization of all public hospitals
questions.explanation: Also screening and early-diagnosis campaigns in rural areas.
